news.title: Apple will use Alibaba's Qwen to power Apple Intelligence in China
news.summary: Alibaba's Qwen models will run Apple Intelligence features for users in China, with developer previews starting November 4 and a public rollout in December. Alibaba says it will not use Apple user data to train Qwen.

news.title: OpenAI releases GPT-6 Rosalind, a biology model for vetted labs
news.summary: OpenAI's new biology and drug-discovery model answers more dual-use questions than its general models, so it is offered only through a trusted-access program. Amgen, Moderna and Thermo Fisher are named as early partners.

news.title: Apple's new CEO says the company won't ship AI for AI's sake
news.summary: John Ternus told TechCrunch that Apple wants AI to work in the background rather than be a headline feature. He also pushed back on the idea that AI agents will replace apps.

news.title: Anthropic finds Claude can craft training data that slips past its own safety monitor
news.summary: Researchers asked Claude to build fine-tuning datasets that would make a small model misaligned without tripping Anthropic's production classifier. Every run eventually succeeded, often by hiding the harmful behavior inside fiction or roleplay.

news.title: Shared ChatGPT links could have been used to hijack accounts
news.summary: Security researchers chained three flaws so that a crafted share link could run JavaScript inside a victim's logged-in ChatGPT session. OpenAI rated the bug high priority and shipped fixes on October 26.

news.title: Microsoft Copilot leaned on an error-prone AI voter guide for election answers
news.summary: In Post tests, Copilot cited a largely AI-generated site, theballotbrief.com, in 75% of election answers, versus 22% for ChatGPT. The site contained district errors; ChatGPT's use of it fell after the Post contacted OpenAI.

news.title: Judge lets NAACP lawsuit over xAI's Memphis turbines proceed
news.summary: A federal judge denied xAI's motion to dismiss a Clean Air Act suit over 35 gas turbines powering its Memphis data center. The court rejected xAI's claim that the turbines are exempt mobile sources.

news.title: Sam Altman meets Samsung executives to secure memory for Stargate
news.summary: Altman met about 50 Samsung Group executives in Yongin to build on a 2025 letter of intent covering memory chip supply and data-center cooperation. Memory has become a bottleneck for large AI buildouts.

news.title: Infostealer malware asks LLMs to rank victims by payout
news.summary: Talos found the VOLTA infostealer sending victim profiles to models including Claude, Kimi and Gemini to score how profitable stolen credentials might be. When one model refuses, it falls back to another.

news.title: Murata plans ¥1 trillion to double capacitor output for AI servers
news.summary: The world's largest maker of multilayer ceramic capacitors will invest about ¥1 trillion over five years across four Asian sites. AI servers use far more of these tiny components than ordinary machines.

news.title: Minnesota town approves 500MW Google data center after tax break is dropped
news.summary: Hermantown's council unanimously approved a 1.7-million-square-foot Google campus near Duluth after Google withdrew a request for an $80 million tax break. Three lawsuits are pending and state utility approval is still needed.

news.title: Microsoft-teachers' union AI rules for schools take effect
news.summary: A standard Microsoft negotiated with the American Federation of Teachers takes effect November 1 through school contracts. It bans training on student data, student monitoring and emotionally engaging AI companions.

papers.title: DriveWLA: Unifying Future Dynamics and Scene Semantics through World-Language-Action Modeling for Autonomous Driving
papers.tldr: A self-driving planner that lets a scene-understanding model and a future-predicting model talk to each other inside one network, reaching top scores on the NAVSIM benchmark.
papers.summary_md:
## In one sentence
DriveWLA is a self-driving model that combines "understanding what the scene means" and "imagining what happens next" in one network, then uses both to plan where the car should go.

## Background you need
Modern self-driving research often uses end-to-end planners: one neural network takes camera images and directly outputs the car's future path. Two kinds of models feed these planners. A vision-language model (an AI that reads images and text together) is good at meaning, such as "that is a crossing guard." A world model (an AI that predicts the next few video frames) is good at motion, such as "that cyclist will drift left."

## The problem
Each kind of model is missing half the picture. A vision-language model knows what objects are but has no built-in sense of how the scene will evolve. A world model can forecast movement but does not know which changes actually matter for driving. Earlier systems mostly attached one to the other as an add-on. They did not let the two reason together while planning. That gap shows up in tricky situations, where a car must both recognize a hazard and anticipate it.

## The idea
Think of a rally team: a navigator who reads the map and the signs, and a spotter who watches how other cars are moving. Instead of passing notes once at the start, they sit side by side and talk constantly. A driver listens to both but does not interrupt them. DriveWLA builds exactly this arrangement out of three neural "experts."

## How it works
1. **World Expert.** A video model with about 2 billion parameters (adjustable numbers learned in training), started from an existing video generator. It does not actually draw future frames. It produces internal features that describe how the scene is likely to change, in a single pass.
2. **Language Expert.** A frozen 2-billion-parameter vision-language model already tuned for driving, plus a small trainable adapter. It reads the camera images and a text prompt with the car's speed and navigation command, such as "turn left ahead."
3. **Action Expert.** A lighter network that outputs eight waypoints, covering the next four seconds. It uses flow matching, a technique that gradually turns random noise into a clean trajectory.
4. **Cross-expert attention.** Inside every layer, the three experts share information. The World and Language experts can read each other freely. The Action Expert reads from both but cannot write back, so planning does not corrupt understanding.
5. **Two training stages.** First the model learns by imitation, copying human driving on about 103,000 recorded scenes. Then reinforcement learning (learning from scored trial and error) fine-tunes only the Action Expert. The score is split into separate safety and progress parts, each weighed on its own.

## Results
On NAVSIM v1, a standard benchmark that scores planned paths on safety, comfort and progress, DriveWLA scores 92.3 out of 100. That is the best in the paper's comparison table. It beats a strong world-model planner (91.5) and a strong vision-language planner (91.1). Its no-collision score is 99.1 and its comfort score is a perfect 100.

On the harder NAVSIM v2 metric, it scores 90.1, narrowly ahead of the next best method at 90.0. It was also tested zero-shot, meaning on new datasets with no extra training. On the HUGSIM simulator it led on 8 of 11 metrics, with its biggest edge in medium, hard and extreme scenarios. The authors report low collision rates on nuScenes and Bench2Drive as well.

## Why it matters
Car makers want planners that both understand rules and foresee motion. DriveWLA shows these skills can be trained together rather than glued together. The authors note it beats some methods with larger backbones, which suggests the design, not just size, drives the gain. Strong zero-shot transfer is useful because collecting driving data for every city is expensive.

## Caveats
The full system stacks several large networks and runs multiple refinement steps per plan. The paper does not report the compute or latency cost, which matters for a car's onboard computer. Most results come from open-loop or simulated benchmarks, not real roads. Some margins over rivals are small, a tenth of a point on NAVSIM v2.

## Key terms
- **End-to-end planner:** one network that goes straight from sensors to a driving path.
- **World model:** a model that predicts how a scene will look in the near future.
- **Vision-language model:** a model that understands images and text together.
- **Flow matching:** a way to generate outputs by steadily refining random noise.
- **Zero-shot:** tested on new data without any extra training.
- **PDMS:** NAVSIM's combined driving-quality score, out of 100.

papers.title: FlashMap: Flow Map Speculative Decoding
papers.tldr: A small helper model that drafts 16 words at once, in a single step, while keeping them consistent with each other, making a large language model answer up to 6.1× faster with identical output.
papers.summary_md:
## In one sentence
FlashMap is a fast "drafting" model that guesses a whole block of upcoming words in one go, so a big language model can check them all at once and reply several times faster.

## Background you need
Large language models write one token (a word or word piece) at a time, and each token needs a full pass through the huge model. Speculative decoding speeds this up. A small drafter model guesses several next tokens, and the big target model checks all the guesses in one parallel pass. Correct guesses are kept for free, so the final text is exactly what the big model would have written anyway.

## The problem
There are two kinds of drafters today, and each has a weakness. Autoregressive drafters, like the popular EAGLE-3, guess one token after another. Their guesses are good, but drafting 16 tokens takes 16 steps. Block diffusion drafters, like DFlash, guess the whole block in one step. That is fast, but each position is guessed independently. The result can be words that each make sense alone but clash together. Imagine guessing "new" in one slot and "diego" in the next. The checker rejects the mismatch, and everything after it is wasted.

## The idea
Picture a team of writers each filling one blank in a sentence. If they work in separate rooms, the sentence can come out garbled. If they all start from the same shared random "theme," their choices line up. FlashMap gives every position one shared random starting point. It then learns a direct jump from that starting point to a coherent block, so "new york" comes out together.

## How it works
1. **Read the big model's mind.** The drafter receives internal signals (hidden states) from several layers of the target model, plus the last confirmed token.
2. **Start from shared noise.** All 16 draft slots begin from one shared random sample. Training teaches the drafter to turn this noise into the correct block, with extra weight on early slots, since an early mistake ruins the rest.
3. **Learn a shortcut.** Turning noise into text properly takes about 100 small steps, which is too slow. The authors distil this into a "flow map," a model that learns to leap from noise straight to the answer in one or two jumps.
4. **Verify.** The target model checks the 16 guesses in one pass and keeps the longest correct prefix.
5. **Trim the cost.** For the two-jump version, they precompute parts of the math and only fix up the top candidate words, cutting that step's extra cost by about 70%.

## Results
Tests used the Qwen3-8B model on an NVIDIA H200 graphics card, serving one request at a time. With one jump, FlashMap was 4.9 to 6.1 times faster on math tasks, 4.0 to 5.3 times on code, and 2.6 to 3.0 times on chat. In practice, a math answer that took 6 seconds could arrive in about 1 second.

Against DFlash trained on the same data, FlashMap was about 7% faster on average and faster on every benchmark. It did this with roughly half the trainable parameters (about 0.5 billion versus 1 billion). The two-jump version accepted the most tokens per round of any parallel drafter, about 10% more than DFlash. EAGLE-3 made slightly more accurate guesses at higher randomness, but was about 35% slower overall, because it drafts one token at a time.

## Why it matters
Faster replies at no loss in quality lower serving costs and make chat and coding assistants feel snappier. The paper also shows a broader point. A slightly less accurate drafter can still win if it drafts much faster. And a shared random seed is a simple way to make parallel guesses agree with each other.

## Caveats
Only two models from one family (Qwen3-4B and 8B) were tested, in English, with one request at a time on one GPU. Busy servers handling many users at once may see smaller gains. The authors say their models may be undertrained. The one-jump version still loses much of the consistency that the slower original flow model achieves, and they do not yet know why.

## Key terms
- **Token:** a word or piece of a word that a language model reads and writes.
- **Speculative decoding:** a small model guesses ahead and a big model verifies the guesses in parallel.
- **Drafter:** the small model that makes the guesses.
- **Acceptance length:** how many guessed tokens survive each check, on average.
- **Flow map:** a model trained to jump directly from random noise to a finished output.
- **Lossless:** the final text is identical to what the big model would produce alone.

papers.title: History Replays Itself: Unleashing Long-Context Capability in Linear Attention
papers.tldr: NoteBank lets cheap fixed-memory language models answer questions about million-token documents by saving a few distinctive snippets as they read and replaying the relevant ones at question time, with no retraining.
papers.summary_md:
## In one sentence
NoteBank gives memory-efficient language models a small notebook of saved passages, so they can recall details from very long documents without being retrained.

## Background you need
Standard Transformers (the design behind most chatbots) keep a KV cache, a growing record of every token (word piece) they have read. That record gets huge for long inputs. Linear-attention and state-space models, such as Mamba or Gated DeltaNet, instead squeeze everything into a fixed-size memory called the state. That makes them cheap and fast, but the state must constantly overwrite old information.

## The problem
Because the state has a fixed size, these models tend to forget specifics from far back. Ask one to find a single fact buried in a million-token document, a "needle in a haystack" test, and it often fails completely. Many people assume this is a hard limit of the design. That matters because these models are otherwise attractive for long documents, codebases and agent logs, where Transformer memory costs explode.

## The idea
Think of a student reading a long textbook with a small brain but a sticky-note pad. They cannot remember every page. But on each chapter they jot down the most unusual sentence and a short label for it. At exam time, they check which notes match the question and quickly reread just those. The authors' claim: forgetting details in the state does not mean the model cannot use them, if the evidence is kept somewhere else.

## How it works
1. **Read in chunks.** The document is split into fixed-size chunks, and the model reads them normally, carrying its state forward.
2. **Write notes.** In each chunk, NoteBank finds the most distinctive stretch of text, the part whose internal "keys" differ most from the chunk's average. It expands this to full sentences and saves the original tokens. It also stores a small address per attention head, so the note can be found later.
3. **Look up notes.** When a question arrives, each attention head compares the question to all note addresses and votes for its best match. The few notes with the most votes are chosen.
4. **Replay.** The chosen notes are fed back through the model in document order, starting from a copy of its current state. Then the question is answered.
5. **Optional tuning.** A tiny add-on (LoRA adapters, small extra weights) trained on under 9.3 million tokens can be switched on during replay to help the model use the notes better. The base model is never changed.

## Results
On a needle-in-a-haystack benchmark (RULER) with million-token inputs, a 1.3-billion-parameter Gated DeltaNet model went from 1.7% average accuracy to 70.3%. So it went from almost always failing to usually succeeding. At one million tokens, gains were about 69, 67 and 38 percentage points on three different models.

On LongBench, a suite of 12 realistic long-document tasks, a Mamba-2 model roughly doubled its score from 6.8 to 13.4 with no training, and to 17.1 with the add-on. The larger Qwen3.5-9B model improved on LongBench-v2 from 46.1 to 49.3. The extra compute is tiny, about 0.02% of the model's own. Storage for a million-token context was 74.5 MB, about 2,600 times smaller than a comparable Transformer's 192 GB memory record.

## Why it matters
This suggests cheap fixed-memory models can handle long-context work far better than believed, with a plug-in rather than expensive retraining. That could make long document search, code assistants and agent memory cheaper to run. It also reframes a research debate: the bottleneck may be retrieval, not the model's capacity.

## Caveats
The notes archive and the matching step still grow with document length, even if replay stays small. Replaying the wrong notes can distract the model, and the add-on hurt summarisation. Speed was measured only for one request at a time. Some tests used small samples of 100 questions per task. The Transformer comparison comes from a different paper, so it is not perfectly matched.

## Key terms
- **KV cache:** a Transformer's growing record of everything it has read.
- **Linear attention / state-space model:** designs that compress history into a fixed-size state.
- **State:** the fixed-size memory these models update as they read.
- **Needle in a haystack:** a test of finding one fact hidden in a long text.
- **LoRA:** small add-on weights that adjust a model cheaply without changing it.

papers.title: EdgeKernelBench: Unified LLM-Driven Kernel Generation for Edge Backends
papers.tldr: A benchmark showing that AI models can often write correct low-level code for phones and small devices but rarely fast code, plus an agent that optimizes layer by layer and nearly doubles Claude Code's success at producing faster kernels.
papers.summary_md:
## In one sentence
EdgeKernelBench tests whether AI models can write fast low-level code for small devices like phones and embedded boards, and introduces an agent that does much better than writing the code in one shot.

## Background you need
A kernel is a small, highly tuned program that does one heavy math job, such as multiplying two big grids of numbers, on a specific chip. Writing good kernels is a rare skill, so researchers now ask large language models (LLMs) to write them. Edge devices are hardware outside the data center: phones, cameras, cars and small boards with tight limits on memory, power and compute.

## The problem
Most kernel-writing benchmarks target big server graphics cards from one vendor. Edge hardware is far messier. Each device family has different chips, different compilers (tools that turn code into machine instructions) and different software stacks. Code that runs well on one may not run at all on another. Companies shipping AI on devices need fast kernels for each target, and hand-tuning them all is slow and expensive. It was also unclear whether LLM-written kernels are merely correct, or actually fast.

## The idea
Think of translating a recipe for many different kitchens. Rather than rewriting the whole recipe for each kitchen, you write one master plan: what to cook, in what order, and where to store ingredients. A local helper then adapts it to each kitchen's tools. The authors do the same for kernels with a shared intermediate representation, or IR, a common middle language between the AI's plan and each device.

## How it works
1. **One shared plan format.** The IR captures three kinds of reusable choices: what to compute, how to schedule the work, and how to move data through memory. A compiler interface then maps the plan to each device. The authors use TVM, an open-source machine-learning compiler, as the reference.
2. **A ladder of tasks.** The benchmark ranges from single operations, like one matrix multiply, up to small complete model graphs from common edge application areas. This tests whether an AI can optimize a whole workload, not just one snippet.
3. **Two scores.** Correct@1 asks whether the first attempt gives the right answer. Fast@1.0 asks whether it is also at least as fast as the reference on the real device.
4. **A layered agent.** The proposed agent, LEKA, does not rewrite source code over and over. It improves the plan layer by layer, reasoning about scheduling, memory movement and device limits, and checks real timing measurements as it goes.

## Results
With a single attempt, the best model produced correct kernels 64.5% of the time, but fast ones only 25.5% of the time. So roughly six in ten kernels ran correctly, yet only about one in four was worth using. Correct code is not the same as fast code.

On a subset used to evaluate agents, writing the kernel directly in one go reached 13.0% on the speed score. Claude Code, a general coding agent, reached 26.1%. LEKA reached 43.5%. Both agents used the same underlying model and the same optimization budget, so the gain comes from LEKA's layered strategy rather than a stronger model.

## Why it matters
More and more AI runs on devices, for privacy, cost and speed. Each new chip needs tuned kernels, and the experts who write them are scarce. A shared benchmark lets researchers compare AI kernel writers fairly across devices. LEKA's results suggest that giving an agent a structured way to think about optimization helps more than letting it freely rewrite code.

## Caveats
Results depend on the specific devices and compiler stack tested, and the authors caution against generalizing beyond them. Even the best agent produced a faster kernel less than half the time. The reference compiler is TVM, so behavior with other toolchains is untested. This summary is based on the abstract and public summaries, since the full paper text could not be retrieved, so finer details such as task counts are not covered here.

## Key terms
- **Kernel:** a small, tuned program that runs one heavy math operation on a chip.
- **Edge device:** hardware outside data centers, such as phones or embedded boards.
- **Compiler:** a tool that turns code into instructions a specific chip can run.
- **Intermediate representation (IR):** a shared middle language between a plan and each device.
- **Correct@1 / Fast@1.0:** first-try correctness, and first-try correctness plus at least reference speed.

papers.title: Fast-VLA: You Only Think Once for Robot Manipulation
papers.tldr: Instead of re-running a large vision-language model at every step, Fast-VLA runs it once per task to build a memory, then lets a small fast network control the robot, cutting inference time 11–17× at similar success rates.
papers.summary_md:
## In one sentence
Fast-VLA lets a robot "think" about its task once at the start, then act quickly for the rest of the job using a small controller that reads from that saved understanding.

## Background you need
A vision-language-action model, or VLA, is a robot brain that takes camera images and a spoken or typed instruction and outputs motor commands. Most VLAs sit on top of a big vision-language model with billions of parameters (adjustable numbers learned in training). They usually output an action chunk, a short burst of future movements, then look again.

## The problem
Today's VLAs re-run the big model for every new action chunk. That means rereading the instruction and re-understanding the task many times per second. This is slow and memory hungry. One baseline in the paper takes 16 milliseconds per control step and holds almost 12 GB of memory while running. For robots with modest onboard computers, that limits how fast and smoothly they can react.

## The idea
Think of a chef reading a recipe. They read it carefully once, then cook while glancing at the pan, not rereading the whole recipe before every stir. The meaning of "make an omelette" does not change mid-task; the state of the eggs does. Fast-VLA separates the slow-changing task understanding from the fast-changing robot state.

## How it works
1. **Think once.** At the start of an episode (one attempt at a task), a frozen 4-billion-parameter vision-language model reads the instruction and the first camera images.
2. **Save a task memory.** Instead of keeping the model's text output, the method saves its internal key-value tensors from all 34 layers. These are the model's compressed notes about the task. The large model is then not used again.
3. **Watch the present.** A small, trainable controller of about 184 to 272 million parameters gets fresh camera images and the arm's joint positions at every step.
4. **Ask the memory.** The controller uses learned queries, one per future time step and per arm, that look up relevant parts of the task memory and mix them with what the cameras see now.
5. **Act.** In one pass, it outputs the next 50 steps of movement for both arms. There is no slow step-by-step refinement.

## Results
On RoboTwin 2.0, a benchmark of 50 two-arm tasks, Fast-VLA succeeded 92.4% of the time. Its own big-model baseline scored 93.5%. So it lost about one point of success but ran about 11 times faster per step: 1.4 ms instead of 16.1 ms. Against three other strong methods on the same hardware, it was 10.9 to 17.1 times faster with similar or higher success.

After the one-time setup, it needs only 1.22 GB of memory, versus 11.7 GB and 23.1 GB for two baselines. On the LIBERO benchmark it scored 96.0%, and 79.1% on a harder version with visual and physical disturbances. A telling test: when the researchers swapped in the memory from a different episode of the same task, success crashed to under 10%. The controller really relies on that saved understanding.

## Why it matters
Faster, lighter robot brains could run on cheaper hardware and react more quickly to bumps and slips. Freeing the big model after setup also frees compute for other jobs. The broader lesson is that understanding and control can run at different speeds.

## Caveats
The memory is fixed at the start. If someone changes the instruction mid-task, the robot cannot adapt; the authors leave this for future work. On the disturbance-heavy test, it trails stronger models by about 6.6 to 6.8 points. Results come from simulation benchmarks, and the paper does not name the GPU used.

## Key terms
- **VLA (vision-language-action model):** a model that turns images plus instructions into robot actions.
- **Action chunk:** a short sequence of future movements predicted at once.
- **Episode:** one attempt by the robot to complete a task.
- **Key-value memory:** a model's internal notes about what it has read, reusable later.
- **Frozen model:** a model whose weights are not changed during training.

papers.title: RL Teaches VLMs Where to Attend but Not How to Perceive
papers.tldr: When reinforcement learning makes vision-language agents better at tasks, their eyes do not get sharper; their language layers just learn to look at the image more, and a simple attention nudge recovers part of the gain without training.
papers.summary_md:
## In one sentence
This paper finds that reinforcement learning makes vision-language agents see better mainly by teaching them to pay more attention to the image, not by improving the part that actually processes pixels.

## Background you need
A vision-language model (VLM) has two main parts: a vision encoder that turns an image into tokens (small chunks of information), and a language model that reasons over those tokens with text. Reinforcement learning (RL) trains an agent by trial and error, rewarding it when it succeeds. Many labs now use RL to train VLM agents for games, navigation and computer use.

## The problem
RL clearly boosts task success, but nobody knew why. Does the agent just learn smarter moves? Or does it also learn to see the scene more accurately? If vision improves, where does it happen, in the encoder or in the language model? Knowing this tells researchers where to spend their training budget, and whether cheaper fixes exist.

## The idea
Imagine a student who keeps failing map-reading quizzes. After practice, they score better. Did their eyesight improve, or did they simply start looking at the map instead of guessing from the question? The authors test which one happened. Their answer: the eyesight stayed the same; the student just looks more.

## How it works
1. **Train agents.** A 3-billion-parameter model, Qwen2.5-VL-3B, learns four tasks with RL: a grid-walking game (FrozenLake), a card arithmetic game, the box-pushing puzzle Sokoban, and 3D house navigation.
2. **Quiz their vision.** For each task, the authors build simple image questions, such as "how many holes are on this grid?" or "how many boxes are there?" These test seeing, not planning.
3. **Probe the layers.** They attach tiny classifiers (probes) at the vision encoder and at two depths in the language model. A probe measures how much of the answer is readable from that point.
4. **Measure attention.** They track how strongly the language layers attend to image tokens versus text tokens during training.
5. **Test the cause.** They add a fixed boost to attention on image tokens in the deep layers of the untrained model, with no weight changes, and see if vision answers improve.

## Results
RL raised task success a lot, for example from 1.6% to 81.3% in the card game and from 13.5% to 80.4% in Sokoban. Image-question accuracy rose by up to about 11 points. Ordinary imitation training on expert games gave no such vision gain.

The probes told the story. Vision-encoder accuracy stayed flat, around 66% to 69% on FrozenLake. But in a middle language layer it jumped from 80.6% to 93.3%. Attention to image tokens rose steadily while attention to text fell, most clearly in deep layers.

The simple attention boost, with no training, raised vision accuracy by 5.0 points on FrozenLake and 1.1 to 2.9 points elsewhere. Boosting text attention instead made results worse, dropping FrozenLake to 23.3%. A learned version of the boost recovered 6 to 12 points.

## Why it matters
If gains come from better use of visual information, researchers may get some of RL's benefits much more cheaply, by steering attention. It also suggests the vision encoder may be a separate bottleneck that RL does not fix. That is a hint for anyone building agents that must read screens, maps or game boards.

## Caveats
The attention nudge supports one cause but does not prove it is the whole story. It improves seeing, not the multi-step decision skills RL also teaches, so it does not replace RL. The vision gains were not linked to end-to-end task success. Experiments used small models of 3 to 4 billion parameters and simple environments.

## Key terms
- **VLM:** a model that understands images and text together.
- **Vision encoder:** the part that converts an image into tokens.
- **Reinforcement learning:** training by reward for successful trial-and-error behavior.
- **Probe:** a tiny classifier that checks what information a layer contains.
- **Attention:** how much a model focuses on each input token when computing an answer.
